answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1905–1997 · Viennese neurologist, psychiatrist & founder of logotherapy
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Frankl, and unusually easy to check. It is in Part One of Man’s Search for Meaning — the camp memoir Ilse Lasch translated from his 1946 German book — and we read it on p. 104 of the scanned 1963 Washington Square Press printing. In the book it is not a standalone maxim but the end of a longer sentence about men who gave away their last piece of bread.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Man’s Search for Meaning: An Introduction to Logotherapy
Part One, “Experiences in a Concentration Camp” — p. 104 in the 1963 Washington Square Press printing
Part One translated by Ilse Lasch
German, Vienna, 1946; in English as From Death-Camp to Existentialism, Beacon Press, 1959

source.excerpt: They may have been few in number, but they offer sufficient proof that everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one’s own way.
trail: We read the sentence in the book. The scanned 1963 Washington Square Press printing ↗ carries it on p. 104, inside Part One (“Experiences in a Concentration Camp,” pp. 3–148), immediately after the passage about men giving away their last piece of bread.

That edition’s own front matter credits “Part One translated by ILSE LASCH,” gives the original title as From Death-Camp to Existentialism, notes that both editions were originally published by Beacon Press, and carries “Copyright, ©, 1959, 1963, by Viktor E. Frankl” (same scan ↗).

The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for the 1959 Beacon Press edition ↗ lists it as Boston: Beacon Press, 1959 and as a translation of Frankl’s German concentration-camp memoir, matching the publication history given for the book on Wikipedia ↗.

Nothing contradicts it: Quote Investigator has no article on the phrase, and Wikiquote ↗ lists no disputed or misattributed entry for it — the wording appears there only inside a 2023 essay quoting Frankl.
source.excerptNote: The famous words are the end of a longer sentence. The “they” are the men Frankl had just described walking through the huts comforting others and giving away their last piece of bread — quoted alone, the line loses the evidence it was drawn from.

author.name: Viktor Frankl
author.heading: About Viktor Frankl
author.bio: Viktor Emil Frankl was a Viennese neurologist and psychiatrist who founded logotherapy, the school of psychotherapy built on the idea that the primary human drive is a search for meaning. Deported in 1942, he survived Auschwitz and a satellite camp of Dachau; his wife and mother did not. The short memoir he wrote afterwards — published in Vienna in 1946 and in English from 1959 — became one of the most widely read books of the century, and made him a fixture on lecture circuits and, eventually, on motivational posters.

misattribution.heading: A real quote with fake company
misattribution.intro: This one is authentic, which makes it unusual for a name this heavily quoted. The problems around it are not invention but drift: a famous line that is not Frankl’s travels alongside it, the sentence is routinely re-cut, and the date attached to it belongs to a book written in another language.

items.scope: “Between stimulus and response there is a space…”
items.who: Stephen R. Covey, credited to Frankl
items.why: Constantly quoted as Frankl’s and often paired with this line. The Viktor Frankl Institute ↗ says it did not come from Frankl: Covey recounted finding it in a library book and thinking it fitted Frankl’s views, but never noted the book’s author or title. Wikiquote ↗ files it under Covey with the note that it is widely and incorrectly attributed directly to Frankl.

On p. 104 of the 1963 edition ↗ the words are the tail of a longer sentence about the few men who comforted others and gave away their bread — they “offer sufficient proof that everything can be taken from a man but one thing…” The familiar version promotes a subordinate clause to a maxim by capitalising “Everything.”

The 1946 book is in German. This English wording is Ilse Lasch’s translation of Part One, first published in the United States in 1959 as From Death-Camp to Existentialism — see the Beacon Press catalogue record ↗ and the book’s publication history ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: the quotation is real. Viktor Frankl wrote it, and you can read it on p. 104 of the scanned 1963 printing ↗ of Man’s Search for Meaning. What is not real is the “space between stimulus and response” line so often quoted beside it.

context.heading: A conclusion, not a slogan
lead: Frankl has just posed a hard question to himself: were the inmates of the camps simply the product of their surroundings? He answers it with something he watched rather than something he theorised — the handful of men who walked the huts comforting others and handing over their last piece of bread. They were few, he says, and that is exactly the point: a few were enough to prove the thing could be done. The famous sentence is the conclusion he draws from them.

Quoted alone it reads as an aphorism about attitude, which is how it ended up on a million posters. On the page it is narrower and harder: Frankl is not saying circumstances do not matter — the surrounding pages are about apathy, irritability, and men who did become “the plaything of circumstance.” He is saying one specific freedom survived, and that some people used it.
detailsBody: Frankl wrote in German. His memoir was published in Vienna in 1946, and the English wording everyone quotes is Ilse Lasch’s translation, first published in the United States in 1959 as From Death-Camp to Existentialism (Beacon Press) and reissued from 1963 under the title Man’s Search for Meaning. So the thought is Frankl’s and the sentence is Frankl’s, but the particular English cadence — “the last of the human freedoms” — is a translator’s choice, as it is with any translated author.
That also means dating the quotation to 1946 and then quoting it in English is a small mismatch. The 1946 book is German; this sentence, in these words, dates from the English translation.
context.pull: He reached it by watching men give away their last piece of bread — not by writing a maxim.

sourcesVerified.claim: The sentence appears verbatim on p. 104 of the 1963 Washington Square Press printing of Man's Search for Meaning, in Part One, following the passage about men who walked through the huts comforting others and giving away their last piece of bread.

That edition's front matter states 'Part One translated by ILSE LASCH', gives the original title as From Death-Camp to Existentialism, notes both editions were originally published by Beacon Press, dates the Washington Square Press edition's 1st printing to February 1963, and carries 'Copyright, ©, 1959, 1963, by Viktor E. Frankl.' Its contents page places Part One, 'Experiences in a Concentration Camp', at pp. 3-148.

The Internet Archive catalogue record for From Death-Camp to Existentialism gives the publisher as Boston, Beacon Press, the date as 1959, and describes the work as a translation of Frankl's German concentration-camp memoir, with Part One 'Experiences in a Concentration Camp' at pp. 1-93.

Wikipedia gives the German original as Ein Psychologe erlebt das Konzentrationslager (Vienna, 1946) and the first English translation as From Death-Camp to Existentialism (Beacon Press, 1959), with Part One translated by Ilse Lasch.

Wikiquote's Viktor Frankl page does not list this wording in its sourced Man's Search for Meaning section — it appears only inside a 2023 essay by Yotam Marom quoting Frankl, under 'Quotes about Viktor Frankl' — and the page attributes 'Between stimulus and response lies a space' to Stephen Covey, noting it is widely and incorrectly attributed directly to Frankl.

The Viktor Frankl Institute states that the 'between stimulus and response' quotation did not originate with Frankl: Stephen R. Covey recounted finding it in a library book he thought fitted Frankl's views, but did not note the book's author or title.
Quote Investigator has no article investigating the phrase 'last of the human freedoms' — a site search returns no results.
